preamble: Denasalization of the nasalized open vowel [ã] to oral [a], usually with the conditioning nasality simply lost. In Middle French, nasal vowels lost their nasality before a nasal consonant that was kept (Old French [fãmə] > [famə] femme); in Galician the Old Galician-Portuguese nasal vowel of lãa, irmãa was denasalized (la, irmá), whereas Portuguese kept it (lã, irmã); and in Lithuanian the nasal vowel written ą, from Balto-Slavic *an, became a long oral [aː] in most dialects in the late 17th and 18th centuries.

examples.note: Middle French denasalized nasal vowels before /m/ or /n/ followed by a vowel; the same development explains the /a/ of couenne, solennel and adverbs in -emment.
The nasal vowel lost its nasality and the two vowels merged into a long [aː]; Portuguese keeps the nasal in lã.
Standard Galician has an oral long vowel; Portuguese keeps irmã with a nasal vowel.

examples.from: Old Lithuanian žąsis with nasal ą [ãː] (< Proto-Balto-Slavic *źansís)
examples.note: The ogonek letter ą once marked a nasal vowel; it now marks a long oral vowel.

examples.from: Old Lithuanian kąsti with nasal ą [ãː] (< Proto-Balto-Slavic *kanˀstei)
examples.note: The ogonek is kept in spelling as an etymological length mark.
